pedagogy.summary: Subtracting multiples of ten (70−30) is taught through unitising: a decade number is a count of tens, so 70−30 is seven tens minus three tens, and the answer is four tens. The known single-digit fact (7−3=4) is reused at the scale of tens. Ten-rods, bead strings and number lines that jump in tens make this visible, so the '0' in the answer carries meaning rather than being appended as a trick.
bestPractices: Build on 'the multiples of ten represent one-to-nine tens': treat 70−30 as 7 tens − 3 tens (NCETM Spine: derived facts, e.g. 30+70 from 3+7)
Reuse the known within-ten fact explicitly — connect 7−3 to 70−30 so the child sees the same subtraction at a larger unit
Represent with ten-rods and with a number line that jumps in tens, so subtraction of tens is a small number of large jumps
Ask the child to explain that subtracting tens is like subtracting the tens digits because each unit is a ten — meaning behind the zero
Contrast 70−3 with 70−30 to expose whether the child is tracking the unit
keyRepresentations: Bead string in tens or 100-bead frame
Number line with jumps of ten
Place-value chart showing the tens column
commonMisconceptions: Dropping the ten-unit: subtracting 7−3=4 and answering 4 instead of 40
Treating the zero as a spelling trick ('add a zero') with no unit meaning
Counting back in ones (70,69,68…) and losing track
Confusing 70−3 with 70−30 because the unit isn't tracked

learn.summary: Teach subtracting multiples of ten (e.g. 70−30) through unitising: a decade number is a count of tens, so 70−30 is seven tens minus three tens = four tens. The known fact 7−3=4 is reused at the scale of tens, so the '0' in 40 carries real place meaning rather than being appended as a trick. Removable tens-materials, bead strings, and number lines that jump in tens make this visible; contrasting 70−3 with 70−30 exposes whether the child is tracking the unit.

activities.title: Removing whole tens from a tens-only mat
feedback: If the child answers 4 for 70 − 30, point to the four rods and ask 'is each of these one, or ten?' — rebuild the answer as four tens = 40.
If the child says 'you just add a zero', ask them to show the four tens on the mat and explain why the answer is four tens and not four ones.
Confirm good reasoning by asking the child to check: add the three removed rods back and see that seven tens (70) returns.
activities.rationale: Unitising — treating 'one lot of ten' as a single object that can be removed whole — is the crux of calculating with numbers larger than ten, and removable tens-materials let the child act on tens as units while watching the count change in ten-steps. An optional linked number line jumping in tens can mirror the rod action.
sourceClaims: Unitising — engaging with 'one lot of ten' as a single entity operated on as one object — is essential for calculating with numbers larger than ten.
learnerActions: Lay out seven ten-rods (or ten-sticks/strips of ten) to represent 70.
For 70 − 30, physically remove three whole rods and say the running count aloud: 70 → 60 → 50 → 40.
Name what is left as 'four tens, which is 40', pointing at the four rods rather than counting individual cubes.
Say the matching single-digit fact: 'seven tens minus three tens is four tens, just like 7 − 3 = 4.'
Repeat for 80 − 50 (eight rods, remove five, leaving three = 30) and 90 − 60 (nine rods, remove six, leaving three = 30), each time removing whole rods and stating the answer in tens.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting multiples of ten is the same subtraction as the known single-digit fact, spoken in units of ten; the zero in the answer is a real placeholder showing zero ones, which keeps the 4 in the tens place. It is not decoration.

activities.title: Contrasting 70 − 3 with 70 − 30
feedback: If the child gives the same answer for both, ask them to lay the two removed amounts side by side (three rods vs three cubes) and compare.
Praise reasoning that references the unit: 'three tens is thirty, three ones is only three.'
activities.rationale: Contrasting 70−3 with 70−30 exposes whether the child is tracking the unit rather than mechanically subtracting digits, directly addressing the confusion between the two.
sourceClaims: Unitising — engaging with 'one lot of ten' as a single entity operated on as one object — is essential for calculating with numbers larger than ten.
learnerActions: Work 70 − 30 by removing three whole ten-rods; record the answer (40) and the running count.
Rebuild 70 with seven ten-rods, then unbundle (or exchange) one ten-rod for ten single cubes; use these to work 70 − 3 by removing three single cubes.
Compare the two results: 70 − 30 = 40 (a big change) versus 70 − 3 = 67 (a small change).
Explain in words why removing three tens changes the number far more than removing three ones.
activities.intendedInsight: The size of the unit being removed matters: subtracting tens and subtracting ones are different because each ten is worth ten ones.

activities.title: Linking the known fact on a reference chart
feedback: If the child writes the answer but reads it as ones, re-read it together as 'four tens'.
Reinforce by asking which single-digit fact each decade subtraction is 'borrowing'.
activities.rationale: A reference layout that pairs the within-ten fact with the decade fact makes the reuse of known facts explicit. This is a scaffold for consolidation and does not by itself let the child act on removing tens, so it works best after hands-on removal.
sourceClaims: Derived-fact reasoning for decade calculations reuses known within-ten facts at the scale of tens (e.g. 86−50 via 80+6−50 = 30+6).
Year 2 pupils derive facts to 100 from facts to 20, e.g. using 3+7=10 to calculate 30+70=100 and 100−70=30; they understand multiples of ten and the value of each digit.
learnerActions: Look at 70 and state that it is '7 tens'.
Do the same for other decade pairs (e.g. 8 − 5 = 3 beside 80 − 50 = 30), reading each as a statement about tens.
activities.intendedInsight: Each decade subtraction reuses a single-digit fact at the scale of tens, so the known fact gives the answer directly.

activities.title: Decade subtraction practice with the dropped-unit trap
feedback: If 4 is chosen, return to the rods: four tens, not four ones.
If the correct answer (40) is chosen but the explanation is 'add a zero', ask them to justify it in tens.
activities.rationale: A short practice set rehearses the strategy and surfaces the dropped-unit error with a targeted trap; it is best placed after hands-on and reference work, which do more to first build the underlying idea.
learnerActions: Complete a short sequence of decade subtractions (e.g. 70−30, 60−40, 90−50), writing each answer.
For 70 − 30, choose the correct answer from options that include 4 as a tempting wrong answer, and explain why 4 is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the tens strategy and catch the common error of dropping the ten-unit.

activities.title: Optional: rhythmic count-back in tens
feedback: Keep this chant focused on jumping in tens for fluency; counting back in ones is still a valid strategy and should not be marked wrong, but for this particular chant gently restart in tens so the ten-jump becomes automatic.
activities.rationale: Rhythmic chanting can reinforce the decade count-sequence and support fluency. It supports but does not build the unitising insight, so it is a supplement to the hands-on work rather than the primary teaching.
learnerActions: Chant the tens count-back sequence aloud with a rhythm: '70, 60, 50, 40' for 70 − 30.
Match the number of jumps to the number of tens being removed.
activities.intendedInsight: The tens count-sequence becomes fluent and the 'jump in tens' becomes a natural move.

constraints: The reference chart and reveal-style layouts are consolidation scaffolds: they link 7−3 to 70−30 but do not let the child remove tens and watch the count change, so they do not by themselves build the unitising action.

Practice sequences and choice items rehearse the strategy and can surface errors such as the dropped ten-unit, so they are well suited to consolidation and checking, and are less likely than hands-on removal to first establish the unitising idea.
Chanting supports the count-sequence; on its own it does not establish why the answer is four tens.

Paper strips, rods, or card tens have slight physical thickness and are approximations of abstract tens; keep attention on 'each piece is worth ten', and an idealised on-screen counter is a model of the tens count, not the tens themselves.
Do not forbid or mark wrong a child who counts back in ones — it is a valid strategy that matures; model the ten-jump alongside it.
Keep the 'subtract the tens digits, keeping the ten-unit' shortcut scoped to decade−decade subtraction; it is not a general rule for cases needing regrouping.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D as 'adding nothing' and framed dialogue as unable to build the insight; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal superiority claims, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.
One source claim (NCETM derived-fact reasoning, used in Activity 3) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its specific worked example as unconfirmed and do not rely on it as proven.

The legacy assessment/correctAnswer uses 'subtract the tens digits keeping the ten-unit' as an efficient method; this is sound for pure multiples of ten but should not generalise to cases requiring regrouping — kept narrowly scoped to decade minus decade.
The value 4 appears in Activity 4 only as a deliberately labelled wrong answer that the child must identify and explain, not as a potentially valid option.

probeDeeper: You said 80 − 50 = 30. Show me with the ten-rods why it's 30 and not 3.
How is 8 − 5 like 80 − 50? How is it different?
What about 80 − 5 — is that the same as 80 − 50? Work it and tell me the difference.
Can you check your answer by adding 50 back to 30?
assess.correctAnswer: 40, 30, 30. Efficient: treat each as tens — seven tens minus three tens is four tens, 40 — or subtract the tens digits keeping the ten-unit (the zero). With rods, remove five ten-rods from eight, leaving three ten-rods = 30.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the ten-unit — 'seven take three is four, so 70 take 30 is 4' — or gets 40 only by 'adding a zero' with no reason
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild with ten-rods so the answer is seen as four tens; name that each digit counts tens, so the zero is a real ten's place, not decoration.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a single-digit answer, or writes 40 but explains it purely as a zero trick with no sense that the digits are tens

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts back in ones — works 70−30 by counting 69,68,67… thirty steps, often losing the count
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT forbid the count-back or mark it wrong — it is a valid strategy that matures. Model 'these are whole tens, so jump in tens' alongside the child's count so the ten-jump becomes the natural move.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child counts back one at a time rather than removing three tens; slow and error-prone on the longer counts

responseLevels.gap: Answers 4 for 70−30, or counts back in ones and loses track; treats the zero as a spelling trick.
responseLevels.full: Answers in tens immediately, explains that subtracting tens is like subtracting the tens digits because each is one ten, and checks by adding back.
responseLevels.partial: Reaches answers with ten-rods in front of them or by counting back, but cannot yet reason 'seven tens minus three tens' without the materials.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set these to work one at a time and watch how the child does them: 70 − 30, 80 − 50, 90 − 60. Then hand them ten-rods and ask them to build 80 − 50 and tell you the answer and how they know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who unitises answers in tens almost instantly and explains '7 tens minus 3 tens'. A child who has lost the ten-unit either counts back thirty ones (and may lose track) or subtracts the digits and drops the ten, saying 70−30=4, or can only justify the zero as 'you add a zero'.
